title: Mirabel and the House
premise: Hospice nurse Wren Vasquez has spent three years ignoring the backwards counting he hears from dying patients, telling himself it's tinnitus, grief, exhaustion. When a voice-activated recorder in his own bedroom captures a second voice answering the count's questions, Wren learns the tally is a harvest: the House on Delmore Street, where he rents a room from the Aldous family, collects a soul every nineteen years and has been counting down to the harvest moon. The dying count backwards because they are being called ahead of schedule, and Wren's name has been entered into the ledger by someone in the family. To survive, Wren must uncover which Aldous made the bargain, expose the truth to the family before loyalty silences them all, and get them out of the House before the moon rises—even though the House does not intend to be empty.
about_author: Xanthe Underhill is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent six years working in end-of-life care before turning to writing full-time. They live in a drafty farmhouse with too many doors and insist, publicly, that none of them open onto anywhere else.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the hospice night shift, Wren tends Mr. Ellery, who counts backwards from one hundred in a voice not quite his own, and dies at nine. Wren documents it clinically, refusing the word 'haunted.' Emotional beat: the practiced numbness of someone who has explained away too much for too long.

chapters.title: A Room on Delmore Street
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren moves his few belongings into the Aldous family's crumbling Victorian, renting cheap from widow Marisol Aldous and her two adult children, quiet Theo and watchful Camille. The House is cold in rooms no one uses. Emotional beat: the fragile relief of belonging somewhere, undercut by the House watching him back.

chapters.title: Static and Second Voices
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. After another patient counts backwards and dies early, Wren sets a recorder by his bed to prove his sleep-talking is ordinary. Playback reveals his own murmured questions—and a second voice, dry as paper, answering each one correctly. Emotional beat: the first crack in three years of denial; fear with nowhere to put it.

chapters.title: What the Voice Knows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The recorded voice knows Wren's childhood address, his mother's maiden name, the date he stopped believing in anything. It calls him 'entry nine.' Wren researches the House and finds a 1943 newspaper clipping: four Aldouses vanished, one returned. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose—he is already in the ledger.

chapters.title: Camille at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. Camille has spent her life keeping the House's rules: salt at the sills, no mirrors facing each other, never answer a voice from upstairs. She notices Wren asking questions and warns him gently, testing whether he's a threat or a fellow prisoner. Emotional beat: loneliness meeting loneliness, guarded but hopeful.

chapters.title: Theo's Silence
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo hasn't spoken above a whisper since he was nineteen—the year of the last harvest, when his father was taken. He repairs the House compulsively, feeding it small obediences. He recognizes Wren's recorder and quietly destroys the memory card. Emotional beat: complicity as a survival strategy curdling into guilt.

chapters.title: Nineteen Years, Nineteen Names
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the county archive, Wren finds a pattern: a death or disappearance on Delmore Street every nineteen years, always near the harvest moon, always someone the family sheltered. The next harvest moon is eleven days away. Emotional beat: the horror of a schedule—this is not haunting but agriculture.

chapters.title: The Dying Speak Backwards
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A new hospice patient, a stranger to the House, begins counting backwards and answers questions Wren never asks aloud. She dies at zero on the harvest moon's eve-minus-eleven, her last word Wren's own name. Emotional beat: grief fused with violation—the count has reached for him through someone else's death.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confesses to the House's attic shrine, not to God: her husband offered a name to save Theo nineteen years ago, and the House took him but kept the debt open, rolling it forward. She wrote Wren's name in the ledger out of desperation, believing a nurse's death would buy Theo's freedom. Emotional beat: a mother's love revealed as the engine of the horror.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. Camille gives Wren the family's survival rules and the truth she's pieced together: the House honors bargains literally, and a name can be struck if freely surrendered by the one who wrote it. But Marisol refuses; striking the name means offering her own. Emotional beat: the crushing weight of loyalty as a cage.

chapters.title: The Voice Gets Closer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The second voice begins speaking from inside the House—through the radiator, the drain, the space behind the wallpaper—asking Wren questions he must not answer truthfully. He lies about his fears; the House tastes the lie and grows colder. Emotional beat: paranoia, the sense that truth itself is the currency being harvested.

chapters.title: What Wren Buried
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Interrogated in his sleep, Wren confronts why he stayed invisible for three years: he once let a patient die alone to protect a lie he told her family, and the guilt made him a man who keeps quiet. The House offers to erase it if he stops digging. Emotional beat: the temptation of comfortable silence, and his refusal of it.

chapters.title: Theo Breaks
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The House, impatient with Marisol's hesitation, starts calling Theo by his father's name. Theo finds his father's coat in the attic, still warm. He confesses to Wren everything he's fed the House for nineteen years and asks, in his first full voice, whether there's any way out that isn't a betrayal. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into desperate courage.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren takes the ledger evidence to the police and a lawyer; both find the paperwork impossibly clean, the archive page blank, his own report misfiled into nonsense. The law cannot see the House. Emotional beat: the institutional abandonment that forces Wren to realize justice here must be made by hand, by family, by choice.

chapters.title: The Night the Doors Moved
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. With five nights left, the House rearranges itself: hallways lengthen, Wren's room migrates toward the cellar, and the front door opens onto the front hall of 1943. Camille maps the House's moods in a notebook, discovering it moves to keep the family apart. Emotional beat: claustrophobic resolve—the House is afraid of them gathering.

chapters.title: Marisol's Refusal
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Wren begs Marisol to strike his name; she refuses, offering instead to finish the original bargain and take Wren's place herself. Wren realizes the House counts any willing name as payment and will never be full. Emotional beat: fury at her sacrifice, and the terrible arithmetic of love versus truth.

chapters.title: The Unmaking of the Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's plan: the ledger is the House's anchor, and a debt dies when every party to it consents to the truth. He gathers the family, reads the 1943 clipping and Marisol's confession aloud, and asks each Aldous to witness it—not to the law, but to each other. Emotional beat: truth-telling as exorcism, fragile and trembling.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The moon clears the treeline and the House begins collecting early, doors slamming shut room by room, the count audible in the walls: ten, nine, eight. The family runs for the front door, which opens onto every year the House has eaten. Emotional beat: pure flight, the climax's ignition, love measured in who looks back.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches Zero
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The House corners Wren at the threshold and offers him the erasure of his guilt one last time. He answers its oldest question truthfully—yes, he was afraid, yes, he was alone—and the truth, freely given, is the one payment the House cannot digest. The count stutters at one. Emotional beat: the climax's turn, surrender as weapon.

chapters.title: What the House Kept
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The House, unable to take Wren, demands its contracted name. Marisol walks back into the hall of 1943 to strike the entry with her own hand, and the House, bound by its literal bargains, must release her—but it keeps the ledger page itself, and something of her with it. Emotional beat: devastating cost; victory that does not feel like winning.

chapters.title: Four of Us, Three Names
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. The survivors—Wren, Theo, Camille—stand in the dawn-lit street as the House goes silent behind them, its door now opening onto an ordinary hallway. They cannot prove anything, press no charges, claim nothing; their justice is simply that they told each other the truth and left together. Emotional beat: battered, incomplete belonging—the family that chose itself.

chapters.title: The Last Patient Counts Forward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, one year later. Wren still nurses the dying, but now he stays in the room, holds hands, and listens. A patient begins to count—forward, one, two, three—and dies at peace at a number of her own choosing. In Wren's new apartment, the recorder stays in a drawer, and nothing answers. Emotional beat: quiet redemption; loyalty and truth finally on the same side.
